Greek comedy emerged in ancient Athens during the fifth and fourth centuries BCE as a form of dramatic entertainment performed at festivals, especially the City Dionysia. Distinct from tragedy, these plays featured absurdist plots, obscene humor, farcical situations, and direct satire of politicians and public figures by name. Old Comedy, the form perfected by Aristophanes, combined political critique with imaginative fantasy: women could rule the world, or an old man could fly to heaven. The stage was a space for impossible wishes and social commentary at once.

Aristophanes dominated Athenian comedy, with his plays surviving in greater number than other ancient Greek dramatists' work. Comedies were performed in competition at civic festivals, giving them public prestige and permission to mock authority directly. Plots often featured impossible premises: women seizing power, ordinary citizens bargaining with gods, wars ended through sexual strike. The humor was heavy on wordplay, obscenity, slapstick, and choral interludes. Physical and bawdy humor worked alongside political commentary.

The Clouds attacks the philosopher Socrates by name for alleged sophistry and corruption of youth—a form of satirical license unknown in modern democratic theater. Lysistrata depicts a sex strike organized by women to end war. It combines crude sexual humor with a surprisingly progressive political argument. Greek comedy also used the parabasis: a choral interlude where the playwright addressed the audience directly, breaking the fourth wall and speaking directly to the people about current affairs.

The decline of Old Comedy after the late fifth century coincided with the loss of Athenian military and political dominance. The form relied on civic confidence and democratic liberty to flourish. When those conditions vanished, so did the distinctive voice of Aristophanic comedy.
